title: Do You Ever Feel Coldhearted Enforcing Consequences? ences/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles the guilt teachers feel when they hold a seemingly remorseful student accountable rather than granting a second chance. He argues that giving in to pleading is a mistake every time, since a warning already functions as a built-in second chance within a well-designed classroom management plan. He lists several consequences of inconsistency: eroded trust, an opening for other students to exploit leniency, unfair case-by-case decision-making, resentment from students who notice favoritism, and an overall increase in misbehavior as students test boundaries. Despite feeling uncomfortable or even 'coldhearted,' Linsin insists that following through is actually an act of compassion — protecting every student's right to learn and proving the teacher is trustworthy. He closes by describing the quiet relief both teacher and class feel when consistency prevails, reinforcing that the world of the classroom 'still makes sense.'
points: Letting a remorseful-seeming student off the hook is a mistake every time, since a warning is already a built-in second chance.
Inconsistent enforcement of consequences erodes student trust and invites more students to test boundaries.
Deciding accountability case-by-case is unfair and provokes resentment among students who notice favoritism.
Following through on consequences, even when uncomfortable, is ultimately an act of compassion and leadership.
Consistent enforcement reassures the whole class that fairness and predictability govern the classroom.
quotes: But letting students off the hook is a mistake. It’s a mistake every time .

A second chance is already built into the classroom management plan we recommend here at SCM. Its purpose is to give students an opportunity to take care of it on their own and without a true consequence.
Each time you go back on your word and fail to do what you promised—in this case, following your plan as it’s written—your students will trust you less and less.
Children have an acute sense of fairness. So when they see you letting some students off the hook and not others—regardless of your reasoning—they’ll resent you.
The truth is, though it may sometimes feel like it, it isn’t coldhearted. Rather, it’s an act of compassion to care enough about your students to make the tough decisions.
You’ll have proven once again that you mean what you say, that you’re a person of your word, and that you can be trusted.
